stem: One sphere has a radius of ${=fixed(a/10, 1)}$ cm and a second sphere has a radius of ${=fixed(b/10, 1)}$ cm. Find the total surface area of the two spheres, in $\text{cm}^{2}$, correct to 1 decimal place. Use the value of $\pi$ on your calculator and round only at the end.
solution: The surface area of a sphere is $A=4\pi r^{2}$. Work out the surface area of each sphere, then add the two areas.

Add the two areas, keeping $\pi$ exact until the end: $\begin{aligned}A_{1}+A_{2}&=({=fixed(4*a*a/100, 2)}+{=fixed(4*b*b/100, 2)})\pi\\&={=fixed((4*a*a+4*b*b)/100, 2)}\pi\\&\approx{=fixed(4 * pi * (a * a + b * b) / 100, 1)}\end{aligned}$
Therefore the total surface area of the two spheres is approximately ${=fixed(4 * pi * (a * a + b * b) / 100, 1)}\text{ cm}^{2}$, correct to 1 decimal place.
notes: Advanced gap. Every book question of this objective is a single sphere with a whole-number radius given directly (we10, ex13-4-1d, ex13-4-3, ex13-7-9), so there is no book exercise that is harder in kind. The honest harder form that stays inside the book's own method is: the same formula 4*pi*r^2 applied twice (two spheres, one-decimal radii) and the two areas added, with a single rounding at the end. It uses the 'total surface area ... correct to 1 decimal place' wording of ex13-4-1d, which is why that is the parent. Nothing new is taught: no diameter, no hemisphere, no volume, no reverse (find r from A). Radii run from 1.2 to 5.9 cm with no whole-number radius; the second radius differs from the first. The stem tells the solver to use the calculator pi and round only at the end, because rounding 4*pi*r^2 per sphere before adding can move the last digit. The require clause keeps the exact total at least 0.002 away from a rounding boundary (checked over all 1818 admissible (a, b) pairs: the 1-dp answer is identical for pi = 3.14159, 3.1416 and the full-precision value). The intermediate coefficients (54.76, 23.04, 77.80 ...) are exact two-decimal numbers because they are 4*r^2 with r in tenths. No distractors: the objective has no catalogued misconceptions and this is a numeric family, not an mcq. If a reviewer judges two-sphere totals to be outside 'surface area of a sphere from its radius', the family should be dropped rather than replaced, since a single sphere with a decimal radius would be standard tier, not advanced.
